Here is the transcript cleaned up for readability, with speakers labeled and filler words removed while preserving all content:

# Dissertation Committee Meeting — Chapter 3 Presentation

---

**Keitaro:** Okay, so in my third chapter, I study how large organizations adapt to employee exits generated by military conscription. Specifically, I study the Tokyo civil service during wartime World War II: when an office loses an employee because they get drafted, how do they fill that position? I focus on the internal labor market side — how do they poach incumbent workers from other offices to fill that role — and distinguish it from the external hiring margin.

To do this, I construct a novel personnel record covering the universe of employees in the Tokyo civil service from 1928 to 1963. It's very rich data. I have the exact positional details of each worker, their peer composition, their salary, and some biographical details such as residential address. For identification, I compare adjacent offices that vary by the number of employees drafted out, controlling for shared organizational structure.

**Committee Member:** What do you mean by "adjacent offices"?

**Keitaro:** They belong to the same office jurisdiction — the same department. The Tokyo civil service had a nested structure where each office was nested into a larger department. I compare offices nested within the same section.

**Committee Member:** You need to say that more precisely. It could mean different buildings, different locations — you need to be explicit.

**Committee Member:** Also, for draft probabilities, wouldn't you need to condition on age? They're probably not drafting 60-year-olds. Shouldn't it be something like occupation by section by age?

**Keitaro:** I don't observe age in the dataset, but I do control for where workers were assigned and what jobs they were working on.

**Committee Member:** So the hope is that job assignment is specific enough to proxy for age?

**Keitaro:** Yes.

**Committee Member:** I mean, to the extent that after controlling for that there's unlikely to be residual heterogeneity by age — that seems reasonable. I don't have strong views either way.

**Keitaro:** So, my main findings: workplaces relied much more on internal transfers than external hires. A one-unit increase in the number of draftees caused twice as many internal hires as external hires. The internal hires were much more concentrated in offices close to the impacted office. I also find evidence that workplaces issued more promotions to retain staff.

**Committee Member:** When you say "closer sections" — do you mean within the nested hierarchy?

**Keitaro:** Yes.

**Committee Member:** You can't use that phrase without defining it precisely — it has too many possible meanings. And being precise also gives you more information about mechanisms. You also need to think carefully about what's mechanical versus what's endogenous. One story is that because of skill overlap, people transfer to closer offices. Another is that the rules simply give closer sections first priority. Both are fine, but you want to know which is true.

For example, when you find transferred workers outperform their peers, is that effect different for closer versus more distant sections? In the closer-section case, they're more likely to be informed about the worker — there's more interaction. The question is: are they ruling out lemons through selection, or is it matching? My prior is that it's all on the selection margin, and you want to provide evidence of that. The more information an office has about a worker, the more likely they are to select good ones — and the more likely those workers are to outperform.

Related to that: do workers have discretion over whether to accept a transfer? Are the promotions and bonuses being given to better performers at the origin office? Are they using promotions and bonuses to target and retain the best workers? You want to distinguish: did we fail to retain Russell because we didn't offer him enough? That's the kind of mechanism you want to identify.

**Committee Member:** On the internal transfers point — it would be useful to decompose how many came from the same higher-node unit. One story is simply that a centralized assignment mechanism exists and the head of the unit just tells people to move. If all the internal transfers come from the same unit, that's useful to know versus transfers coming from further away. It's partly a descriptive thing, but it helps clarify whether this is coming from the top or not.

**Keitaro:** Yes. So I decompose the internal transfers by how close the origin office was — same department versus different department — and I find that the 0.41 coefficient decomposes into 0.26 from the same department and 0.14 from different departments.

I also find that transferred workers outperform their peers. Comparing transfer workers to peers at the origin office, I estimate their chances of having a good career — measured by tenure and post-war survival — are substantially higher, as are rank gains.

**Committee Member:** Are the transferred workers younger than those who stayed at the donor office? That could explain the tenure effects. It would be useful to compare characteristics of transferred workers versus those who stayed.

**Committee Member:** That's why you also want to look at how they performed at the donor office before the transfer.

**Committee Member:** Right. And conditioning on closeness — if they're within the same group, where there's presumably more information, do you see bigger tenure effects? That would be very hard to reconcile with a pure age story. The other issue, even conditional on age: what does transferring signal about preferences? Workers who actively seek career moves within the organization may be more devoted to the organization or more ambitious. That could be correlated with productivity but could also just reflect individual preferences. That's going to confound measures of productivity that are based on staying in the institution.

**Keitaro:** To address some of those questions, I compare transferees sent to a draft-impacted office against transferees sent to an office that lost someone due to a voluntary exit. I still find a positive effect on all four outcome measures.

**Committee Member:** What counts as a "natural exit"? Excluding retirement — just moving to another office?

**Keitaro:** I'm including both exit from the Tokyo civil service and exit from the workplace, but I can distinguish those two.

**Committee Member:** What was that last row you skipped?

**Keitaro:** There I'm comparing with peers at the destination office. It's a bit tricky because the composition of peers at the destination is endogenous to drafting.

So to summarize: I find the internal hiring margin mattered much more than the external hiring margin during wartime. I also find that transferred workers appear to have accelerated their career trajectories as a result of this forced exit mechanism, contributing to better outcomes later on.

**Committee Member:** I'm not sure how you distinguish that from selection — even after controlling for comparing them with other transferred workers. Suppose you find they performed better before and better after. All that may show is that you selected better workers. You can't easily separate that from your interpretation of accelerated career trajectories. It's the same problem as comparing people hired under different conditions — the people hired under condition B may just be a different kind of recruit. Especially with tenure and promotion-based measures of productivity, there's a real concern about selection on preferences to stay at the firm.

**Committee Member:** You can get at some of it by separating out cases where the organization is plausibly better informed versus less informed. If they're within the same hierarchy, they probably know more about the worker. Can you check whether, in close-hierarchy transfers, there is particularly strong negative selection on prior performance at the origin — i.e., are they avoiding people who performed badly? Other measures of closeness beyond the organizational chart would also help: how much interaction these sections might have based on their functions, physical proximity of offices, whether managers ever worked in the same section. If two section heads previously worked together, they'll share information more than the org chart alone would suggest. Those alternative measures of closeness would strengthen your identification of the mechanism.

**Committee Member:** I'll say this: where you started on this paper, I thought it was a no-hoper, and you figured that out eventually — after I hit you over the head with it countless times. But I think this has real promise. You just need more time on this paper.
